title: There is now an alternative to Russian gas – but not yet to soaring prices
content:
According to GIE AGSI, the public gas storage platform for European gas infrastructure, Slovakia is currently receiving 486 GWh of gas per day, while withdrawals are approaching 615 GWh daily. With the heating season under way, an increasing share of these withdrawals is going directly to household consumption.

The energy content of the gas currently in storage stands at 20.5 TWh, representing 54.28% of Slovakia’s maximum gas storage capacity. This is below both Hungary’s storage level (77.5%) and the EU average (75%). Only Latvia has a lower figure in the statistics, at 50%.

At the same time, Slovakia’s storage capacity relative to its consumption is considerably higher than the EU average. Of the 3.5 billion cubic metres that can be stored, the majority – approximately 2.75 billion cubic metres – is held in NAFTA’s storage facilities near Láb, close to the Austrian and Hungarian borders.

These facilities are ideally positioned to receive and store both Russian gas arriving via TurkStream through Serbia and Hungary – at least for the time being – and gas delivered from Austria, including LNG unloaded at terminals in northern Germany.

title: “What Are They Not Telling Us?” Reminders to Prepare for Emergencies Fuel Anxiety About an Impending Crisis
content:
The posts claim that these announcements were made almost simultaneously and ask whether this means the whole world is preparing for war or another crisis. However, as Delfi’s investigation shows, some preparedness recommendations have been in place in many countries for years, while more recent information campaigns are linked to specific national civil protection and societal resilience plans, rather than an impending global catastrophe.

In October this year, posts began circulating on X, Threads and other social media platforms claiming that numerous countries around the world were, one after another, urging residents to prepare so-called 72-hour emergency bags or stocks of essential goods and supplies that would allow them to manage for at least three days without outside assistance. Reports that the US Department of Defense was planning to prepare military bases to operate for three months without external support added fuel to the fire.

These posts have reached very large audiences in a short time. For example, a post by an account called Whale News Daily on X has received more than 5.3 million views.

content:
Latvia’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) describes this narrative as part of the aggressor state’s information warfare, while military expert Mārtiņš Vērdiņš also says that, for now, it is a false alarm.

“Latvia currently faces no direct military threat,” says Ministry of Defence.

“Russia’s Defence Ministry is preparing to send reservists to territories along NATO countries’ borders, in what would be the largest deployment since the start of the so-called “special military operation”. Putin has approved the creation of a huge troop deployment corridor in north-western Russia. It is planned to stretch from Karelia to the Kaliningrad region. title: Former World Bank economist accuses Baltic States of irresponsibility but gets his facts wrong
content:
In one of them, the economist also links the Baltic States’ historical experience to the risk of the rest of the world facing a nuclear apocalypse. His original post garnered at least 621 000 views in just over a week.

“It is a strange world. Because three small Baltic countries have a population of 5.7 million (and a combined area smaller than that of some second-tier Chinese city), half of whom live in Europe, while another third are Russians who cannot obtain citizenship, and because they have trauma and bad memories of Soviet rule, the entire world of eight billion people is supposed to head towards a nuclear apocalypse and perish,” Branko Milanović wrote on X on the 19th of October.

After the post was published, people from the Baltic States pointed out factual inaccuracies, including questioning the population and ethnic composition figures he cited. Commenters also said that Milanović’s remarks echoed Kremlin propaganda narratives.

In response to the criticism, Milanović published another post on 22 October, clarifying that his original post had referred to ethnic Russians rather than non-citizens.

title: Ukrainian could become Lithuania’s second official language – fake news circulated in the names of officials
content:
A fabricated news item circulating on Lithuanian social media appears to show President Gitanas Nausėda and Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys expressing views on the possibility of granting Ukrainian the status of a second official language. How was it established that the material was generated by artificial intelligence?

The fake report claims, citing alleged statements by Nausėda and Budrys, that they do not rule out the possibility of Ukrainian becoming Lithuania’s second official language and being made compulsory in schools.

According to Delfi.lt, the image circulating on social media attempts to imitate an article published by the news portal 15min, but was created using artificial intelligence. This is evidenced not only by the fact that the man pictured next to the president bears little resemblance to the foreign minister, but also by a digital watermark embedded in the image.

title: Many EU countries have special anti-corruption agencies – but their very existence may signal systemic problems
content:
Experiences across EU countries shows that specialised anti-corruption agencies can play a crucial role in tackling political corruption, but their effectiveness depends on institutional independence and political will. While some countries have successfully prosecuted senior politicians, others continue to struggle with political interference, weakened law enforcement institutions and lengthy judicial proceedings. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office is becoming an increasingly important player in protecting EU funds and strengthening accountability.

Article:

  • Specialised anti-corruption agencies are not a solution in themselves. Their effectiveness depends on political independence, sufficient investigative powers and a functioning justice system.
  • The nine EU countries take different approaches to fighting corruption. Romania, Latvia and Lithuania have dedicated anti-corruption bodies, while Finland relies on cooperation between existing institutions.
  • Political interference remains a major obstacle. Recent institutional changes in countries such as Slovakia, Hungary, Poland and Bulgaria demonstrate how strongly anti-corruption efforts can depend on government priorities.

title: Czech-Polish Dialogue Forum: A Fragmented Defence Industry, Dependence on Washington, and the War Europe Refuses to Call by Its Name
content:
The continent has capable armed forces, excellent engineers, and innovative companies, yet struggles to bring these resources together into a coherent force. The answer, they argued, lies not in another round of political declarations, but in concrete procurement orders, joint projects, and political agreement on priorities. Whether Europe can achieve any of these things remains an open question.

The problem was most forcefully articulated by Jan Farský, a Member of the European Parliament and the European People’s Party’s rapporteur on the AGILE programme. “Europe is not weak. It is just fragmented,” he said. The continent, he argued, was losing its potential through national disputes, despite possessing capable armed forces, excellent engineers, and innovative companies. European countries continued to plan, purchase, and manufacture largely along national lines and outside the EU framework.

title: The “silence of the bots” never came: what is Ukraine trying to achieve by bombing data centres in Russia?
content:
Kirils Solovjovs, a cybersecurity expert and head of the Possible Security group of IT security companies, told Delfi that bombing data centres can make life harder for the population of an aggressor state and disrupt resource-intensive artificial intelligence operations, but so-called “bots” can easily be moved from one server to another. Meanwhile, Cert.lv, the institution responsible for internet security in Latvia, shared with Delfi that it has observed no changes in Latvia’s online environment attributable to the bombing of Russian data centres.

Ukraine has been striking the backbone of the Russian economy – its oil refineries – with large-scale drone attacks for more than a year. This summer, warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, were added to its list of favoured targets. In early October, Ukrainian drones inflicted serious damage on a data centre belonging to Russian technology giant Yandex in the Ryazan region for the first time. Several more strikes on Yandex computing centres followed, after which Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles also bombed data centres belonging to Sberbank and the social media platform VKontakte.

title: Lavrov’s close ally Szijjártó at the centre of a new scandal as his ties to Chinese carmaker investigated
content:
Péter Szijjártó served as Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade in Viktor Orbán’s government for more than 11 years, from September 2014 until the 9th of May 2026. The defeat of Orbán’s Fidesz party in the parliamentary election held on 12 April brought an end to his 16-year dominance of Hungarian politics.

The new Prime Minister, Péter Magyar, quickly set about reviewing the policies of the previous pro-Kremlin government and investigating potential wrongdoing.

Orbán’s government had already earned a poor reputation for attempting to block aid to Ukraine and the adoption of European Union (EU) sanctions against Russian individuals and legal entities.

However, in March, shortly before the parliamentary election that would prove fatal to Orban’s political fortunes, reports emerged that Szijjarto had been informing Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov for years about discussions at EU meetings. The Washington Post was the first to report the allegations, writing that Szijjarto had regularly called Lavrov during breaks in meetings.

title: Slovakia restores military contacts with Russia at attaché level. What does this actually mean?
content:
Although Bratislava has vigorously defended the move, critics have warned of espionage risks and further erosion of trust between NATO member states.

Robert Fico secured an agreement to resume military attaché activities in May, when the Slovak leader visited Moscow to mark Victory Day and met with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin. He was the only European Union (EU) leader to attend the 9th of May celebrations in Moscow this year and last year. Aktuality reports that, sitting opposite Putin at a large table in the Kremlin, Fico promised that Slovakia would resume cooperation with Russia at military attaché level.

But what does this actually mean? In this context, a military attaché is a military officer assigned to work at their country’s embassy abroad. The officer is responsible for military and defence cooperation matters, maintains contacts with the host country’s military leadership, and monitors developments in the military and political situation.

Slovak Defence Minister Robert Kalinak has now implemented the agreement, according to Slovak media. Slovakia has sent two military officers to Moscow, while one Russian officer has been sent to Bratislava.

title: European countries to launch major defence projects. What role will Latvia play?
content:
Drones, air defence, satellites, and the security of the eastern border are receiving increasing attention. To strengthen cooperation between countries in these areas, five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCIs) were approved at the end of September at a meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council in its Defence Ministers’ configuration. 

The concept behind these projects was introduced with the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP), adopted by the EU in 2025, the Council of Europe explains. These are joint industrial projects designed to help develop Member States’ military capabilities that are essential to the EU’s security and defence interests. Such projects enable EU Member States to undertake major and complex defence initiatives collectively, which would be too large-scale or complicated for any one country to develop on its own. 

The projects are: 

Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER) – the project will help European countries develop, scale up and deploy drones, as well as technologies to neutralise adversary drones, thereby addressing critical gaps in the participating countries’ defence capabilities.
